Introduction/AI-SDLC

Development guide

EDS AI-SDLC

The EDS AI-Software Development Lifecycle (AI-SDLC) connects Project Discovery, implementation and learning from use. Project Discovery investigates needs and tests possible responses. A delivery agreement defines what to build next. Implementation builds and checks that scope before release; evidence from use informs the next decision.

Product, Design and Engineering collaborate throughout. Delivery findings can change the proposed solution or reopen the problem; bounded fixes can start from existing requirements. This overview explains the end-to-end flow, responsibilities, evidence and decisions. The Project Discovery playbook separates theory from Maya’s story. Product Implementation explains the delivery method independently of its continuous worked example, which follows Maya’s pilot from requirements to release and learning.

One lifecycle, two connected learning loops

Project Discovery asks whether the problem is worth solving and which response deserves the next investment. Implementation asks whether the change meets the agreed intent and what happens when people use it. Both loops create evidence that can change the next decision. Read the flow from Project Discovery to the delivery agreement, implementation, release and learning; use the linked chapters for detailed methods and the continuous learning journey.

A shared readiness agreement connects the loops through a product requirements document (PRD), supporting evidence, technical findings, user interface (UI) artefacts where relevant and current organisational context. Feedback from delivery and use keeps the agreement open to revision.

The two loops compared
AspectProject DiscoveryProduct implementation
Question it answersAre we making the right product?Are we making the product right?
Starts fromA problem, user need, strategic priority or new capabilityAgreed behaviour and acceptance criteria, supporting evidence and organisational context; a bounded fix may use existing requirements and an issue record
LoopFrame (steps 1–2), Test (3–4), Decide (5), Prepare delivery (6)Plan, slice, implement, verify, release and observe, learn

What it improvesThe product intentThe product and the way the team builds it

Explore each loop below, then follow its detailed guidance.

The MINDEF and DSTA Defence Product Playbook’s ProductOps flywheel connects research, repeated design and testing, and concurrent DevSecOps work. This guide applies that iterative principle through its Project Discovery and implementation loops.

Project Discovery: decide what is worth building

Use Project Discovery when the problem, expected value, proposed experience or technical feasibility is uncertain. Product, Design and Engineering use Frame → Test → Decide to investigate needs, compare responses and test assumptions. Start with the question you need to answer and check whether existing evidence still applies.

The authorised decision owner records the findings, their limitations and what to invest in next. The team may continue testing, revise the approach, defer or stop, depending on what it learns. When the evidence justifies building a limited scope, prepare the next delivery slice with testable requirements, linked findings, measures and owners for remaining questions.

Draft the PRD when the team needs to describe the proposed behaviour in detail. It is not required for every Project Discovery test.

Explore the six practical steps in Project Discovery.

Agree the next delivery slice

The handoff connects learning with a bounded delivery commitment. Product, Design and Engineering agree the useful scope to build, the evidence supporting it and how the result will be judged. Keep them involved as implementation exposes new information.

A shared package carries the product requirements document (PRD), relevant UI or interface artefacts, validation and technical findings, current organisational context, and a measurement plan. It describes the intended outcomes, scope and exclusions, acceptance criteria, dependencies and remaining uncertainty. Link the source records rather than making separate copies for each stage.

Check readiness together

The receiving team checks that the behaviour is testable and the designs cover critical interactions. Review evidence for user value, usability, technical feasibility and viability within the bounded scope. Record missing constraints, measurement work and unresolved questions. Resolve questions that could invalidate the scope before dependent work; name an owner, next check and escalation trigger for accepted uncertainty.

The authorised investment owner records the commitment and its limits. This permits the next delivery work; production release needs separate implementation and operational evidence, reviewed through the applicable release decision.

Use Project Discovery’s detailed handoff and measurement guidance, then implementation’s readiness checks.

AIHow AI can help

AI can assemble a draft handoff summary and flag missing criteria or evidence links. Product, Design and Engineering compare it with the source records, resolve gaps and retain the reviewed package with the commitment decision.

Product implementation: deliver and verify the intent

Use implementation when the next change has agreed behaviour and testable acceptance criteria. Link requirements to relevant design decisions, tasks and verification evidence using records appropriate to the change. A PRD and technical requirements document (TRD) carry product intent and technical decisions; a bounded defect or maintenance change may use existing requirements and its issue record.

The six activities are Plan → Slice → Implement → Verify → Release and observe → Learn, with rework and feedback throughout. Passing checks provides evidence that the change meets agreed criteria under recorded conditions. Independent reviewers compare the results with the agreed criteria and identify any failures. The authorised decision maker then decides whether to accept the quality report and remaining risk for the defined scope or return the work for correction.

Release follows applicable criteria and the authorised release decision, with limited exposure, monitoring, stop thresholds and recovery arrangements. Evidence from use then helps the team assess whether the expected benefit is emerging. Compare results with the agreed outcomes and technical assumptions, then update the relevant requirements, design decisions, tasks or context. Findings can reopen Project Discovery at any point, including during planning.

Explore implementation: stage inputs, evidence and exit decisions.

Use evidence to choose the next action

Compare observed results with the intended user outcome, acceptance criteria and operating guardrails. Investigate why the results differ before deciding which loop needs attention.

Feedback signals and decisions
SignalFirst responseDecision to record
Behaviour violates agreed criteriaCorrect and independently verify the implementation; contain live impact where necessaryCorrection, evidence and any release or recovery action
Expected benefit is absent or unclearCheck measurement quality, exposure, adoption, observation period, task mix and operating conditionsCorrect delivery or measurement issues, gather more evidence, or reopen Project Discovery to test product assumptions
New evidence challenges scope or constraintsAssess affected work and involve the relevant decision authority; use Project Discovery to compare alternatives where neededContinue with authorised changes, narrow, pause or stop affected work
Review queue grows or agent changes wait longer than expectedCheck change size, work in progress, review capacity and whether consequential judgement was delayed until code reviewSlice work smaller, add pairing or a design review, or rebalance review capacity; retain independent checks and acceptance criteria
A defect or delay recursAddress the immediate issue and investigate contributing delivery conditionsPreventive change to context, tools, tests or review practice, its owner and a check for recurrence

These routes can overlap. Product, Design and Engineering review the evidence together and name an owner to coordinate the response. Record the finding, evidence links, next action and review trigger. Distinguish that coordinating owner from whoever holds authority to change scope, accept risk or approve release under the applicable local arrangements.

DORA recommends making user feedback available to the team and displaying user measures alongside technical measures. Use that evidence to revisit priorities, rather than treating faster output as proof of value. [1]

Further reading: diagnose a value measure that stops improving

A stalled measure does not mean the team has failed, but something is holding it back. The Defence Product Playbook suggests finding the cause before changing the plan.

Likely causes of a stalled value measure, adapted from the Defence Product Playbook
Likely causeHow you can tellAction
The root cause is not addressedUsers adopt the product, but the problem persistsRevisit the problem statement in Project Discovery
An assumption was falseResearch shows an assumption was wrongPivot the approach in Project Discovery
The problem has changedEvidence shows it shrank or shiftedRedefine or deprioritise the problem
The team is blocked from outsideThe team waits on an approval, decision or access it cannot grant itselfEscalate to whoever holds the blocking decision
The team cannot move fastThe team is active but slow or unfocusedReview its structure, skills and delivery process

The playbook suggests moving investment towards another problem when a plateau means the product has delivered its available value. This handbook adds a diagnostic check: distinguish saturation from measurement limits or changing conditions, and assess essential outcomes and obligations before reducing investment. Maintenance can preserve reliability, supportability and risk controls even when the headline measure stops rising.

AIHow AI can help

Ask AI to group permitted feedback, defect reports and operating observations with links to the original records. The team checks the proposed groups and their context, then records whether to correct implementation, reopen Project Discovery or improve the delivery process.

Use AI across the lifecycle

AIHow AI can help

AI-assisted development means using AI to support development work; the resulting product does not need to contain an AI feature. People still decide the intended outcomes, acceptable trade-offs and scope of agent activity.

AI can help organise research and challenge assumptions, draft plans and changes, and trace feedback to the requirements and decisions it affects. People remain responsible for deciding what to invest in, accepting work and material risks, and authorising release.

Compare findings that affect the decision with the original research notes or test results. Check whether the AI omitted conflicting evidence, counted the same observation twice or presented an interpretation as an observation. Keep supported findings and source links, and record unanswered questions before using the summary to guide work. Check generated code and tests against the agreed criteria, retaining the results for independent review.

McKinsey’s 10 February 2025 article argues for AI assistance across product development: connect research with usage evidence, test ideas earlier, and consider quality, risk, compliance and accessibility from Project Discovery onwards. Its anticipated benefits are proposals and industry perspectives, rather than proof of improvement for every team.

Hold AI-written work to the same quality bar as any other work. The Defence Product Playbook’s ProductOps Quality Model sets four layers of checks, so that quality does not depend on who or what authored the code:

  1. Prevention, before the build: project rules for agents, reusable design-system components and typed contract boundaries.
  2. Outcome validation, from design onwards: test plans, usability results, scorecards and objectives show whether the work had its intended effect.
  3. Automated scanning, at pull request: composition analysis, static and dynamic scanning and container checks.
  4. Integration verification, after merge: confirmation that the pieces work together.

The playbook argues for preventing defects through the first layer, rather than relying on later scanning. Apply the relevant release criteria alongside these checks. Read how implementation applies gates and independent assurance.

Choose where to go next: Investigate an uncertain problem, value or solution in Project Discovery, or plan, build and verify an agreed change in Product implementation. Use the EDS AI Workflow (Eitri) for the local delivery procedure.
